# Hint cards: catalogue

Generated 2026-11-16 by tools/hints-catalog.mjs from the audit files (.mace/hints/audit-<state>.json, written by tools/hint-audit.mjs). Do not edit by hand.

Every state of the app is a section; each section lists, for every element the audit found, the plain text of its hint card. A card the audit marks "generic" is the old fallback text of the engine and counts as a miss. Elements opted out by Victor have no card, by decision.

### pop-sonification

| Tick sounds | `#sonTicks` | control | Price ticks | Price ticks ○ Neutral: no verdict ticks are on Price ticks On In plain words A two-note chime each time the active pair, EUR/USD , moves by one step: up for an uptick, down for a downtick. The step now is 0.60 pips ; a move over four steps adds a third note. The register follows the distance from the price 24 hours ago. Use it Keep it on for the pair you trade; it follows the pair that is on the chart. |
| Heartbeat | `#sonHeart` | control | Portfolio heartbeat | Portfolio heartbeat ○ Neutral: no verdict the heartbeat is on Heartbeat On 0 open positions In plain words A low two-note pulse every 1.6 s while you hold positions. The pitch follows the open P&L against the equity; the pulse turns tense and doubles its tempo when a position is within a quarter of its stop distance from the stop. It is silent now: nothing is open. Use it It works as an alarm for the stop: a tense pulse means a position is close to its stop. |
| Sonification volume | `#sonVol` | control | Volume | Volume ○ Neutral: no verdict 50% of the sound level Volume 50% In plain words How loud the market sound is, from 0 to 100%. It scales both the ticks and the heartbeat and does not touch the alert beeps. Use it Low enough to work under, high enough to notice a change. |
| Sonification sensitivity | `#sonSens` | control | Sensitivity | Sensitivity ○ Neutral: no verdict a tick every 0.60 pips Sensitivity 1.00× 0.60 pips per tick on EUR/USD In plain words How small a move makes a sound. A tick plays for each step of 0.6 ÷ sensitivity pips on the active pair. A higher value means more sounds. Range rare normal busy 1.00× Use it On a fast pair lower it; on a quiet one raise it. |
| LISTEN TO THE MARKET | `#sonPop > b` | text | Listen to the market | Listen to the market ○ Neutral: no verdict the settings of the market sound In plain words The two sounds the ear button plays and how loud and how sensitive they are. They are based on Janata and Childs (2004): a rising two-note chime is an uptick, a falling one a downtick. Use it Set them once; the ear button switches the sound on and off. |
| Price ticks of the active pair | `#sonPop > label` | text | Price ticks | Price ticks ○ Neutral: no verdict its label · ticks are on Price ticks On In plain words A two-note chime each time the active pair, EUR/USD , moves by one step: up for an uptick, down for a downtick. The step now is 0.60 pips ; a move over four steps adds a third note. The register follows the distance from the price 24 hours ago. Use it Keep it on for the pair you trade; it follows the pair that is on the chart. |
| Portfolio heartbeat (open P&L) | `#sonPop > label` | text | Portfolio heartbeat | Portfolio heartbeat ○ Neutral: no verdict its label · the heartbeat is on Heartbeat On 0 open positions In plain words A low two-note pulse every 1.6 s while you hold positions. The pitch follows the open P&L against the equity; the pulse turns tense and doubles its tempo when a position is within a quarter of its stop distance from the stop. It is silent now: nothing is open. Use it It works as an alarm for the stop: a tense pulse means a position is close to its stop. |

The choices None no cap: every instrument at its sheet leverage EU ESMA: 1:30 on major pairs, 1:20 on other pairs, gold and major indices, 1:10 other commodities and minor indices, 1:5 stocks, 1:2 crypto UK ESMA caps; crypto derivatives are not offered to UK retail AU ESMA caps (AU retail uses the ESMA index list) US NFA: 1:50 on major pairs, 1:20 on other pairs; no CFDs Watch out A change recomputes the margin of open positions; with open trades it shows the new level first and asks. Use it Pick the jurisdiction that applies to you, or None to test with sheet leverage. |
| tkSlipOn | `#tkSlipOn` | control | Slippage | Slippage ○ Neutral: no verdict slippage is on Slippage On σ 0.2 pips · latency 120 ms In plain words When on, a market order fills at a price that can differ from the quote by a random amount: a normal distribution with the σ below, plus the price movement during the latency. A positive deviation is against you. When off, orders fill exactly at the quote. Use it Keep it on: a test without slippage is optimistic. |
| Slippage sigma in pips | `#tkSlipSd` | control | Slippage σ | Slippage σ ○ Neutral: no verdict 0.2 pips σ in pips 0.2 In plain words The standard deviation of the random part of the fill, in pips. About two thirds of fills land within this distance of the quote; larger moves are rarer. Range 0 to 5. Use it The default is 0.2 pip, a calm market; raise it to test a bad fill. |
| Latency in milliseconds | `#tkLat` | control | Latency | Latency ○ Neutral: no verdict 120 ms Latency in ms 120 In plain words The delay between your click and the order reaching the market, in milliseconds. It is randomised between 0.5 and 1.5 times the value, and the price keeps moving during it, so a higher value widens the fill. Range 0 to 2000. Use it The default is 120 ms. |

It is part of the cost of every trade and of the backtests that use the account costs. Range 0 to 50. Use it Set it to what your broker charges; a strategy that only works at zero cost does not work. |

| DEPTH OF MARKET | `#iDom > div.ph > h2` | text | Depth of market | Depth of market ○ Neutral: no verdict the price levels around the market In plain words A ladder of prices: the ask levels above the spread and the bid levels below it. The prices are the real steps of the live quote; the bars are drawn for orientation (see the note under the title). Reading it Above the middle ask levels: where a sell limit rests The middle row the spread and the mid price Below the middle bid levels: where a buy limit rests Use it Click a level to fill the ticket; Shift+click for a stop order. |
| ILLUSTRATIVE DEPTH — FILLS IGNORE SIZE | `#domIll` | text | Illustrative depth | Illustrative depth ● Marginal: needs attention the sizes are drawn, not measured In plain words The price levels follow the live quote, but the bars and the sizes are illustrative : they are drawn for orientation and do not come from the market. A fill never depends on them. What is real and what is not Price of each level real: steps from the live bid and ask Bar length and size illustrative Your orders and stops real: marked on their level Watch out Do not read a long bar as a wall of orders: there is no queue behind it. Use it Use the ladder to pick a price, not to read the market's intent. |
| BID SIZE | `#iDom > div.dom-head > span` | text | Bid size | Bid size ● Marginal: needs attention illustrative size In plain words The size drawn at a bid level, in millions on FX. It is illustrative: it is not the market's queue. Use it Ignore the size when you choose a price. |
| PRICE | `#iDom > div.dom-head > span` | text | Price | Price ○ Neutral: no verdict the price of the level In plain words The price of each level, in steps of the ladder (1, 5 or 10 pips of the step buttons). Use it Read the price, then click the level. |
| ASK SIZE | `#iDom > div.dom-head > span` | text | Ask size | Ask size ● Marginal: needs attention illustrative size In plain words The size drawn at an ask level, in millions on FX. It is illustrative: it is not the market's queue. Use it Ignore the size when you choose a price. |

| CURRENCY STRENGTH | `#iStr > div.ph > h2` | text | Currency strength | Currency strength ○ Neutral: no verdict which currencies moved most, relative to the others In plain words Each of the eight majors is measured by its change against the US dollar over the lookback, then compared with the average of the eight. The result is in basis points (1 bp = 0.01%). USD is measured as zero before the average is taken. How it is built Change log change of the currency against USD Strength (its change − the average of the eight) × 10,000 Lookback 4 hours (the buttons) Watch out It describes the move that already happened. It does not say the move continues. Use it Use it to see which currency is driving a pair, not to pick a direction. |

| SORT | `#monitor > div.ph.mon-ph > button.mon-sortbtn[type=button]` | control | Sort | Sort ○ Neutral: no verdict default order: nothing is ranked Order of the tiles now Default In plain words Chooses the order of the tiles. The ranked orders re-sort when you pick them or change the group; the figures on the tiles keep updating. The four orders Default the order of the instrument list Change the highest 24 h change first, the lowest last Biggest movers the largest 24 h change first, up or down Range vs ATR the 24 h range as a multiple of a typical day (the “× typ” figure on each tile) first In every ranked order, markets that are closed go behind the open ones, so a closed market never ranks as a mover. Read the name carefully “Range vs ATR” ranks by the range against the typical day range (the “× typ” figure), not by the ATR figure. It finds who has used the most of a normal day. Watch out The tile’s “× typ” compares with the five previous days only; an instrument with fewer than five comparable days shows “—” and has no typical day to compare with. In Range vs ATR it is then ranked by its raw 24 h range in pips or points, so it can land among the first tiles without being stretched. Use it Biggest movers finds where price is moving now; Range vs ATR finds who is stretched against its own normal. |

| MOMENTUM · RSI 1H | `#brMain > div.brx-kpis > div.brx-kpi` | text | RSI(14) on 1H | RSI(14) on 1H ● Marginal: needs attention oversold: stretched down RSI(14), 1-hour bars 14 average gain against average loss over 14 bars In plain words Price fell hard and fast: the recent losses far outweigh the gains. A short bounce is likely, but a trend can stay oversold for a long time. Scale oversold normal overbought 14 Watch out RSI is not a reversal signal on its own. | How much each instrument moves: the ATR of one hour against  | `#volBody > div.vol-top > p.vol-intro` | text | What this table shows | What this table shows ○ Neutral: no verdict how much each instrument moves In plain words One row per instrument: how much it moves in an hour ( ATR ), how that compares with its usual for the same hours, how far it travelled in the last 24 hours and where price sits in that range. Press a row to open the instrument on the chart. What the numbers are ATR(14) is Wilder's average true range over 14 complete one-hour bars (gaps included; the hour in progress is left out). An instrument needs at least 15 complete hours of history to be listed. Use it Check it before you set a stop: the ATR column is the size of the noise. |
| ATR | `div.vol-top > p.vol-intro > span.brx-n.term` | text | ATR(14) on 1H | ATR(14) on 1H ○ Neutral: no verdict the size of one hour of movement In plain words Average true range: how much one hour moves, from its low to its high, gaps included . As a % of price it compares a JPY pair, a stock and an index. How it is computed ATR(14) is Wilder's average true range over 14 complete one-hour bars (gaps included; the hour in progress is left out). An instrument needs at least 15 complete hours of history to be listed. Watch out It measures size, never direction. Use it Express stops as multiples of ATR, then size the lots to that stop. |

Above 1.25× the market is busier than usual, below 0.8× quieter. Scale quieter normal busier 1.22× The baseline The baseline is the average true range of the same hours of the day among the earlier bars of the last 101 complete hourly bars (about four days of trading, not a full week). It needs at least 10 matching hours, otherwise the cell shows —. Watch out It is the plain average of the column, so a few instruments can pull it: check the rows before concluding the whole market is moving. Use it Plan as usual; look at the rows that stand out. |

The measure ATR(14) is Wilder's average true range over 14 complete one-hour bars (gaps included; the hour in progress is left out). An instrument needs at least 15 complete hours of history to be listed. The two ends now NZD/USD 0.14% EUR/GBP 0.07% Use it Compare bars to see how much more room one instrument needs than another. |
| % OF PRICE | `#volBody > div.vhead > span` | text | ATR, % of price | ATR, % of price ○ Neutral: no verdict comparable across instruments Highest now 0.14 % NZD/USD In plain words One hour of ATR divided by the last price. It puts a JPY pair, a stock and an index on the same line, which pips and points cannot do. The list ranks by this column. Use it Use it to compare instruments; use the pips column to place a stop. |
| PIPS / PT | `#volBody > div.vhead > span` | text | ATR, pips / points | ATR, pips / points ○ Neutral: no verdict the unit of the order ticket In plain words One hour of ATR in pips for currency pairs and points for CFDs: the unit you set stops and targets in. Watch out A pip is not the same amount of money on every instrument, so do not compare this column across rows. Use it Compare your stop in pips with this number before you send the order. |
| VS WEEK | `#volBody > div.vhead > span` | text | vs week | vs week ○ Neutral: no verdict now against its usual for these hours Average of the column 1.22 × 16 instruments In plain words The hourly ATR now against the average of the same hours of the day earlier in the period, so a busy London afternoon is compared with other afternoons and not with the quiet night. Above 1.25× is flagged as busier than usual, below 0.8× as quieter. Scale quieter normal busier 1.22× The baseline The baseline is the average true range of the same hours of the day among the earlier bars of the last 101 complete hourly bars (about four days of trading, not a full week). It needs at least 10 matching hours, otherwise the cell shows —. Watch out The column is called "week" but the baseline is the last 101 complete hourly bars, about four days. Use it Sort by this column to see what is unusual right now. |
| 24H RANGE | `#volBody > div.vhead > span` | text | 24h range | 24h range ○ Neutral: no verdict high minus low of the last 24 hours In plain words How far the instrument travelled between its high and its low over the last 24 hours, in pips or points. For a market that has been closed for longer, it is its last bar. Use it Compare it with the ATR: a day range of several ATRs means one or more hours were unusually large. |
| % · × 1H | `#volBody > div.vhead > span` | text | 24h range, % and × ATR | 24h range, % and × ATR ○ Neutral: no verdict the same range, in two other units In plain words The 24h range as a % of price, and as a multiple of one hour of ATR . A high multiple means the day's range is large compared with a normal hour. Use it Use the multiple to see whether the day was one big move or many small ones. |
| PRICE IN 24H RANGE | `#volBody > div.vhead > span.l` | text | Price in the 24h range | Price in the 24h range ○ Neutral: no verdict 0% is the low, 100% the high In plain words Where price is now inside the range of the last 24 hours: L is the low, H the high. From 90% it is at the high, up to 10% at the low, and the cell says so. Scale low end inside high end 50% Watch out The ends say where price is, not that it will turn or break. Use it Sort by At an end to find the instruments at the edges. |

What you see The cone a 68% and a 95% band that widen to the right of now Graded against its own past week and a constant-volatility cone Your levels ticket and position stops and targets, with the odds of reaching them Use it Read the calibration first: a cone that missed last week is a softer guide. |

| rgCv | `#rgCv` | canvas | The regime plot | The regime plot ○ Neutral: no verdict every pair placed by memory and randomness In plain words Each dot is a pair. Its horizontal position is the Hurst exponent (persistent to the right, anti-persistent to the left), its vertical position the permutation entropy (more random upward). The grey band is where random paths of the same returns would fall. How to read it Dot inside the band indistinguishable from noise: most pairs, most of the time Dot right of the band trending recently Dot left of the band mean-reverting recently Dot below the band unusually ordered moves Big dot a volatile pair Watch out A dot outside the band describes the recent path. It does not predict the next move. Use it Click a dot to open its pair; then read the side panel for the numbers. |

The windows overlap (each starts an hour after the last), so a zone tends to last about as long as the window itself; it describes the past windows only. How it is counted The window slides one hour at a time. For each hourly window the zone (anti-persistent, noise or persistent) is computed again. The count is how many of the latest windows share today's zone. Watch out The windows overlap, so a zone lasts about as long as the window itself; a long stay is not 25 independent confirmations. Use it A non-noise zone that has lasted for many windows is worth more than one that has just appeared. |

| Currency market only (16 FX pairs): the Observatory, Edge ch | `#pane-obs > p.obs-scope.muted` | text | Scope of the Observatory | Scope of the Observatory ○ Neutral: no verdict what the Observatory covers In plain words Currency market only (16 FX pairs): the Observatory, Edge check and Baskets are built on currencies; CFDs are not part of them. Why it says so The tools are built on the live prices of the currency pairs (and, where stated, other instruments). They are descriptive: they show how the market has behaved, not what it will do. Use it Use the Observatory to understand the market before you trade: what is linked, what is trending, what is quiet. |
| Déjà vu | `#obsHead > div.obs-title > h3` | text | Déjà vu | Déjà vu ○ Neutral: no verdict what this tool answers In plain words Has the last stretch of this pair happened before? The closest shapes in the history of all 16 pairs, what followed them, and whether that ever predicted anything here. What you see The chart the last bars of the pair against what the closest past shapes did next The verdict whether this method called the next move better than a coin, on this pair's own past The list the 12 closest matches, one per moment Use it Read the verdict first. If it says no edge, read the matches as a spread of outcomes, not as a direction. |
| EUR/USD | `#obsHead > div.obs-title > span.obs-sym` | text | EUR/USD | EUR/USD ○ Neutral: no verdict the instrument this tool reads The instrument open on the Trade chart EUR/USD In plain words Déjà vu works on the pair that is open on the Trade chart. It accepts one of the 16 G8 pairs; for another instrument it says so in place of the chart and offers EUR/USD. The rule Tool Déjà vu Accepts one of the 16 G8 pairs Use it Change the pair on the Trade chart or with a pair button inside the tool; the numbers follow it. |
| as of Tue 10:00 UTC | `#obsAsOf` | text | As of | As of ○ Neutral: no verdict the moment of the data Time of the last data point (UTC) Tue 10:00 UTC In plain words Every figure on this page is computed up to this moment. On the weekend it is the last trading minute of Friday: the market is closed and nothing changes. Use it If it is much older than the clock, the market is closed or the feed is down: do not trade on it. |

| Each currency is measured against an equal-weighted basket o | `div.obs-split > aside.obs-side > p.small.muted` | text | How the legs are built | How the legs are built ○ Neutral: no verdict the method, in words In plain words Each currency is measured against an equal-weighted basket of all eight, so a pair's move splits exactly into its base leg and its quote leg. The idea comes from currency research, where a common dollar factor explains much of the moves of the dollar pairs. The rule Basket equal-weighted mean of the eight currencies A currency's leg its move minus the basket's move The pair base leg plus the effect of the quote leg: exactly Use it Because the split is exact, the legs always add up to the pair. |

In this tool Equal weights over USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CHF, AUD, CAD and NZD: the mean of the eight currencies. Use it A currency is "strong" if it moved more than this mean. |

| Constellation Correlation map | `#obs > nav.obs-nav > button` | control | Constellation | Constellation ○ Neutral: no verdict click to open this tool In plain words Which pairs move together right now. A tree of the strongest correlations between the 16 pairs: adjacent = directly correlated; further along a branch is not implied. In the menu Tool Constellation Subtitle Correlation map Use it Before a second trade, check whether both pairs sit next to each other on the map. |
| Regime map Trend or noise? | `#obs > nav.obs-nav > button` | control | Regime map | Regime map ○ Neutral: no verdict click to open this tool In plain words Has each pair's recent path been persistent, anti-persistent or like noise over 1–32 minutes? Every pair is placed by its memory (Hurst) and its randomness (entropy), against the band where the same returns with random signs land. It describes the window; it does not forecast. In the menu Tool Regime map Subtitle Trend or noise? Use it Use it to see which pairs behaved like a trend, a reversal or noise over the window. |

| Constellation Correlation map | `#obs > nav.obs-nav > button` | control | Constellation | Constellation ○ Neutral: no verdict click to open this tool In plain words Which pairs move together right now. A tree of the strongest correlations between the 16 pairs: adjacent = directly correlated; further along a branch is not implied. In the menu Tool Constellation Subtitle Correlation map Use it Before a second trade, check whether both pairs sit next to each other on the map. |
| Regime map Trend or noise? | `#obs > nav.obs-nav > button` | control | Regime map | Regime map ○ Neutral: no verdict click to open this tool In plain words Has each pair's recent path been persistent, anti-persistent or like noise over 1–32 minutes? Every pair is placed by its memory (Hurst) and its randomness (entropy), against the band where the same returns with random signs land. It describes the window; it does not forecast. In the menu Tool Regime map Subtitle Trend or noise? Use it Use it to see which pairs behaved like a trend, a reversal or noise over the window. |

This one also checks whether ea | `#obsBody > div.lab-intro > p` | text | What this tool does | What this tool does ○ Neutral: no verdict a signal with its own track record In plain words Every scanner finds signals. This one also checks whether each signal has actually paid on that pair: it finds every past trigger in the last week of 15-minute bars, then measures the move 2h later. Triggers never overlap, so the t-statistic is honest. A survivor is a hypothesis to test forward, not a signal. The method in the code Past week closed 15-minute bars, up to 700 Triggers the bar where a signal appears; one that merely persists is not a new trigger No overlap the next trigger waits until the horizon is over Baseline the same hour of the day, so a quiet hour is not mistaken for a failure Use it Read the banner, then the verdict of each signal. |

A signal that did not pay on that pair is not a signal there. Use it Check the report card: a signal that paid on one pair and not on the others is weaker evidence than one that paid on several. |

| With 43 signal–pair tests (8+ cases each) and nothing real b | `div.sc-wrap > div.sc-card > p.small.muted` | text | What luck alone gives | What luck alone gives ○ Neutral: no verdict about 2.8 of 43 tests In plain words With 43 signal–pair tests (8+ cases each) and nothing real behind them, about 2.8 would pass \|t\| > 2 by chance. 7 passed — above the chance count, but pairs share currencies so the tests are correlated and the excess can still be luck. How it is computed The sum over the tests of the probability that \|t\| exceeds 2 given that test's number of cases (Student's t). The sentence compares the number that passed with that count. Use it A count close to the expected one is what a market with no edge looks like. |

The rules Yours what you actually did Target 1R / 2R / 3R stop 1R, take profit at that multiple Trail 1R the stop follows the best price at 1R Break-even + 3R stop to entry after +1R, target 3R Time stop 1h / 4h stop 1R, otherwise exit after that time Hold 24h stop 1R, otherwise exit after 24 hours Pricing A buy exits on the bid and a sell on the ask, so a replay pays the normal spread. | ATR × multiple Fixed pips | `#btSlMode` | control | Stop type | Stop type ○ Neutral: no verdict the stop follows the volatility of the signal bar How the stop is placed ATR × multiple every trade has a stop: R is measured from it In plain words Every trade gets a stop at entry. With ATR the distance is the multiple times the ATR(14) of the last closed bar; fixed uses the same distance every time. The stop also sets the position size: the amount at risk divided by the stop distance. ATR(14) Average true range over 14 bars, smoothed (Wilder). After a closed market the first bar counts only its own range, so a reopening gap does not widen the stops. Watch out A fixed stop under 2× the spread is mostly cost; the form shows a warning in red when it is. Use it ATR stops adapt to quiet and busy hours; fixed stops are easier to compare across runs. |
| btSlK | `#btSlK` | control | Stop (× ATR) | Stop (× ATR) ○ Neutral: no verdict stop distance = this multiple of the ATR(14) Stop multiple 2 × ATR the live ATR is not available yet In plain words The stop sits this many ATR(14) from the entry, using the ATR of the last closed bar before the entry (the bar that gave the signal). A wider stop is hit less by noise, and the position gets smaller because the same risk is spread over more distance. What it moves Wider (higher) fewer stop-outs by noise, smaller size, bigger target distance Tighter (lower) more stop-outs, larger size for the same risk Minimum 0.2 × ATR Watch out Target and break-even are in R, so changing the stop changes where they sit in price. Use it Sweep Stop × ATR against Target R in the Optimizer to see how stable the result is. |
| btTpR | `#btTpR` | control | Target (R) | Target (R) ○ Neutral: no verdict no target: trades exit by stop, signal or time Take profit none 1 R = the distance to the stop In plain words The take-profit is placed this many times the stop distance from the entry. 0 means no target. When a stop and a target are both touched in the same minute, the stop is taken first. Break-even win rate Without a target the result depends on the other exits: opposite signal, trailing, break-even, time. Watch out A take-profit fill carries no slippage; a stop fill does. Use it Test it as a sweep: a target that only works at one value is probably noise. |
| btMax | `#btMax` | control | Max bars | Max bars ○ Neutral: no verdict off: no time limit Time exit off In plain words A trade still open after this many bars is closed at the close of that bar (reason "Time exit"), with slippage. 0 turns it off. Use it Use it to stop a trade that has gone nowhere from tying up the account and paying swap. |
| btOpp | `#btOpp` | control | Exit on opposite signal | Exit on opposite signal ○ Neutral: no verdict on: the opposite signal closes and reverses Reverse on the other signal On the exit fills at the next bar's open In plain words When the opposite entry rule fires while a trade is open, the trade is closed at the next bar's open (reason "Opposite signal") and the new one opens on the same bar. Watch out Trades closed this way pay slippage and the spread like any market exit. Use it Turn it off for strategies with a fixed target, where the opposite signal would cut winners short. |
| Off ATR × multiple Fixed pips | `#btTrail` | control | Trailing stop | Trailing stop ○ Neutral: no verdict off Trailing stop type Off it moves only in your favour In plain words Once the trade is in profit by the "Trail from" distance, the stop is held at the best price reached minus the trail distance and never moves back. It is updated for the next minute, never in the same minute, so a bar cannot trail and stop out on its own high. Use it Pair it with a target of 0 to let winners run, or leave the target in place as a cap. |
| btTrailK | `#btTrailK` | control | Trail (× ATR) | Trail (× ATR) ○ Neutral: no verdict only used with an ATR trailing stop Trail multiple 2 × ATR trailing is off In plain words With an ATR trailing stop the distance behind the best price is this multiple of the ATR(14) of the last closed bar. Minimum 0.25. Use it A trail tighter than the stop gets hit by normal noise. |
| btTrailAct | `#btTrailAct` | control | Trail from (R) | Trail from (R) ○ Neutral: no verdict the trail only starts after this profit Trail activation 1 R 0 = from the entry In plain words The trailing stop starts only once the trade has been this many R in profit (the best price reached, in multiples of the stop distance). 0 means from the entry. Use it A start at 1 R keeps the trail from cutting a trade before it has paid its stop. |
| btBe | `#btBe` | control | Break-even at (R) | Break-even at (R) ○ Neutral: no verdict off Break-even trigger off 0 = off In plain words Once the trade has been this many R in profit, the stop moves to the entry price. If price comes back, the trade exits there (reason "Break-even") minus slippage, and still pays commission and swap, so it closes at a small loss, not at exactly zero. Watch out In many strategies a break-even stop turns would-be winners into zero trades: test it with the trail and without. Use it Sweep it against the target before assuming it helps. |
| btRisk | `#btRisk` | control | Risk / trade % | Risk / trade % ○ Neutral: no verdict inside the 5% line of the ticket Equity risked on each trade 1 % the loss if the first stop is hit In plain words The size of each trade is chosen so that a hit on the initial stop loses this share of the current equity, in whole volume steps of the instrument sheet. Equity compounds from $100,000. Against the ticket's limits normal high 1.0% The ticket colours risk amber above 5% and refuses an order above 10% . The backtester accepts 0.05% to 10%. Watch out The size is capped by the leverage, by the per-order cap of 25× equity and by the sheet's maximum; those trades risk less than asked and the result says how many. If the risk asks for less than the sheet's minimum size, the run trades the minimum and the trade risks more than this %. Use it Start at the risk you would really take; the same strategy at a higher risk only scales the drawdown with it. |
| btSlip | `#btSlip` | control | Slippage (pips) | Slippage (pips) ○ Neutral: no verdict a fixed penalty on every market fill Slippage per fill 0.2 pips against you, on top of the spread In plain words Each entry, stop, time exit and opposite-signal exit is filled this far worse than the price. Take-profit fills carry no slippage, and neither does the last close at the end of the data. Watch out It is a constant, not a model of fast markets. Use it Keep it above zero: a result that only works with zero slippage is not a result. |
| btOos | `#btOos` | control | Out-of-sample % | Out-of-sample % ○ Neutral: no verdict the last 30% of the bars are held back as a test slice Share of bars for the test slice 30 % the run itself covers all bars In plain words The run is also measured on the first part (in-sample) and on the last part (out-of-sample) of the bars. The full run, the verdict and the equity curve always use all bars; the split only fills the in-sample table and the shaded area of the curve. 0 turns it off; the maximum is 60. Watch out The slice is cut from the same history; if you pick settings by looking at it, it stops being out of sample. Use it Judge the strategy first by what happens on the slice, then stop tuning. |
| Account costs Declared costs | `#btCost` | control | Costs | Costs ○ Neutral: no verdict the costs this account pays live Cost model of the run Account costs In plain words The run uses the costs this account pays in live trading: the instrument sheet's spread (night 23:00–01:00 server time, Monday to Friday), the swap of each 17:00 New York rollover held, and the sheet's commission plus your extra commission from Settings. Not in the backtest News spread widening is live only: the calendar of the past is not kept. Use it Leave Account costs on to compare with live results; use Declared costs to test a cheaper or dearer account. |
| Account costs · spread 1.2 pip · 1:25 | `div.bt-sec > details.bt-costs.bt-cfgcost > summary.small` | control | Account costs | Account costs ○ Neutral: no verdict what every trade of the run pays Costs and sizing Account costs · spread 1.2 pip · 1:25 the line shows spread and leverage In plain words Account costs, as in live trading: spread 1.2 pip (night 23:00–01:00 server time 2.4 pip), swap −9.217 pts long / −8.771 pts short a night (triple on Wednesday), commission none on the instrument sheet. News widening is live only: not in the backtest. Sizing rules Size in steps of 0.01 lots, from 0.01 lots to 400 lots per order, notional at most 25× equity: the per-order cap of 25× equity is tighter than the 1:500 leverage (No jurisdiction cap). Fills only while the market is open. Watch out A signal before a market close fills at the reopening, and a stop crossed by the gap fills at the reopening price. Use it These are the same costs as in live trading when Account costs is on. |
| RUN BACKTEST | `#btRun` | control | Run backtest | Run backtest ○ Neutral: no verdict one run = one more try recorded in this account What it does Run 0 tries recorded so far In plain words Reads the settings and runs the strategy over the history: the whole run, then the in-sample and out-of-sample parts. With more than one week of history it first fetches the extra weeks. The result and the Verdict appear on the right. What is recorded The run is added to the list of tries (the same settings replace their earlier entry). PSR, DSR and N effective use that list, so every change you try makes a good result harder to believe. Watch out Nothing is sent to the market: it is a test on past prices. Use it Change one thing at a time and read the verdict before the numbers. |
| RUN ON ALL FX PAIRS | `#btAll` | control | Run on all FX pairs | Run on all FX pairs ○ Neutral: no verdict the same settings on every FX pair: each one is a try FX pairs in the run 38 pairs pairs without a live feed are left out and counted In plain words Runs the current instrument first, then the same strategy and settings on each FX pair with a live feed, over the full period, and opens the All FX pairs list. Other instruments are not part of it. Read it carefully The pairs share currencies, so their results move together: it is not that many independent tests. Each pair is still one more try that DSR counts. Use it Use it to see whether an idea works across pairs, not to pick the best pair afterwards. |
| BACKTEST SETTINGS | `#btCfg > h3.bt-band` | text | Backtest settings | Backtest settings ○ Neutral: no verdict a section of the settings In plain words Everything the run needs: the instrument and history, the strategy, the exits, the sizing and the costs. Nothing here touches your account or sends an order. Use it Hover each field of the section for its exact effect on the run. |

From the instrument sheet Distances in pips Spread 1.2 pip (night 23:00–01:00 server time 2.4 pip) Size steps 0.01 lots, from 0.01 lots to 400 lots per order Leverage of the account 1:500 Per-order cap notional at most 25× equity Watch out The test runs on the platform's own 1-minute prices only. With no live feed for the instrument, Run says so and runs nothing. Use it Pick the instrument you actually trade, then compare it with the other FX pairs through Run on all FX pairs. |
| Timeframe 5m 15m 30m 1H | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Timeframe | Timeframe ○ Neutral: no verdict the size of one bar: signals act on its close Bar size of the run 15m the 1-minute prices are merged into bars of this size In plain words The 1-minute prices are merged into bars of this size. A rule is evaluated when a bar closes and the order fills at the open of the next bar. Stops and targets are still checked minute by minute inside each bar. What it changes Lower (5m) more bars, more signals, more trades; each pays the spread Higher (1H) fewer bars and fewer trades; a longer history is needed for the same count Verdict rule under 20 trades the Verdict says "Too few trades to judge"; PSR and DSR need at least 5 Watch out Indicator lengths are counted in bars of this size: EMA 21 on 5m is a different thing from EMA 21 on 1H. Use it Choose it with the History setting: the number of trades is what lets a result mean anything. |
| Direction Long & short Long only Short only | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label.w2` | text | Direction | Direction ○ Neutral: no verdict both sides are traded Sides the strategy may trade Long & short the rules of the other side are ignored In plain words The long and the short rules are both live. If both fire on the same bar, no trade is taken. How it works The check is on every bar close: a long signal is taken only when the direction allows long and the short rules are not true on the same bar, and the other way round. Use it Use Long only or Short only to see which side carries the result. |
| History Live week 4 weeks 8 weeks 12 weeks | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | History | History ○ Neutral: no verdict fetched from the platform when you press Run How far back the run goes 8 weeks not loaded yet In plain words Backtests run on the platform's own 1-minute prices. The live week is the one the chart shows. 4, 8 or 12 weeks fetch the weeks before it from the platform when you press Run (about 1 to 5 seconds a week) and keep them for the session. Options Live week no fetch 4 weeks fetched on Run 8 weeks fetched on Run 12 weeks fetched on Run Watch out If the platform has 1-minute prices only from a later date, the run covers the real part and says so; it never fills the gap. Use it More history means more trades and a fairer verdict; a single week is a thin sample. |

| Stop (× ATR) | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Stop (× ATR) | Stop (× ATR) ○ Neutral: no verdict stop distance = this multiple of the ATR(14) Stop multiple 2 × ATR the live ATR is not available yet In plain words The stop sits this many ATR(14) from the entry, using the ATR of the last closed bar before the entry (the bar that gave the signal). A wider stop is hit less by noise, and the position gets smaller because the same risk is spread over more distance. What it moves Wider (higher) fewer stop-outs by noise, smaller size, bigger target distance Tighter (lower) more stop-outs, larger size for the same risk Minimum 0.2 × ATR Watch out Target and break-even are in R, so changing the stop changes where they sit in price. Use it Sweep Stop × ATR against Target R in the Optimizer to see how stable the result is. |
| Target (R, 0 = none) | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Target (R) | Target (R) ○ Neutral: no verdict no target: trades exit by stop, signal or time Take profit none 1 R = the distance to the stop In plain words The take-profit is placed this many times the stop distance from the entry. 0 means no target. When a stop and a target are both touched in the same minute, the stop is taken first. Break-even win rate Without a target the result depends on the other exits: opposite signal, trailing, break-even, time. Watch out A take-profit fill carries no slippage; a stop fill does. Use it Test it as a sweep: a target that only works at one value is probably noise. |
| Max bars (0 = off) | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Max bars | Max bars ○ Neutral: no verdict off: no time limit Time exit off In plain words A trade still open after this many bars is closed at the close of that bar (reason "Time exit"), with slippage. 0 turns it off. Use it Use it to stop a trade that has gone nowhere from tying up the account and paying swap. |
| Exit on opposite signal | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label.chk` | text | Exit on opposite signal | Exit on opposite signal ○ Neutral: no verdict on: the opposite signal closes and reverses Reverse on the other signal On the exit fills at the next bar's open In plain words When the opposite entry rule fires while a trade is open, the trade is closed at the next bar's open (reason "Opposite signal") and the new one opens on the same bar. Watch out Trades closed this way pay slippage and the spread like any market exit. Use it Turn it off for strategies with a fixed target, where the opposite signal would cut winners short. |
| Trailing stop Off ATR × multiple Fixed pips | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label.w2` | text | Trailing stop | Trailing stop ○ Neutral: no verdict off Trailing stop type Off it moves only in your favour In plain words Once the trade is in profit by the "Trail from" distance, the stop is held at the best price reached minus the trail distance and never moves back. It is updated for the next minute, never in the same minute, so a bar cannot trail and stop out on its own high. Use it Pair it with a target of 0 to let winners run, or leave the target in place as a cap. |
| Trail (× ATR) | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Trail (× ATR) | Trail (× ATR) ○ Neutral: no verdict only used with an ATR trailing stop Trail multiple 2 × ATR trailing is off In plain words With an ATR trailing stop the distance behind the best price is this multiple of the ATR(14) of the last closed bar. Minimum 0.25. Use it A trail tighter than the stop gets hit by normal noise. |

Use it A start at 1 R keeps the trail from cutting a trade before it has paid its stop. |
| Break-even at (R) | `div.bt-sec > div.bt-row3 > label` | text | Break-even at (R) | Break-even at (R) ○ Neutral: no verdict off Break-even trigger off 0 = off In plain words Once the trade has been this many R in profit, the stop moves to the entry price. If price comes back, the trade exits there (reason "Break-even") minus slippage, and still pays commission and swap, so it closes at a small loss, not at exactly zero. Watch out In many strategies a break-even stop turns would-be winners into zero trades: test it with the trail and without. Use it Sweep it against the target before assuming it helps. |

### lab-risk

35 elements: 30 with a card, 0 generic, 5 opted out, 0 misses.

| Element | Place | Kind | Card title | Card text |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Win rate percent | `#lWin` | control | Win rate % | Win rate % ● Marginal: needs attention positive expectancy at this reward : risk Share of trades that win 45 % between 1 and 99 In plain words The chance that any one trade is a winner, the same for every trade. Each simulated trade is an independent draw: a win multiplies equity by 1 + risk × reward : risk, a loss by 1 − risk. Break-even at this reward : risk With a reward : risk of 2.00, the win rate that gives zero expectancy is 1 ÷ (1 + 2.00) = 33.3% . Yours is 45%. Watch out Real trades are not independent draws with one fixed win rate, and a win rate measured on a few trades is uncertain. The form checks this field when you press Run: whole numbers, up to 99. A value between steps is refused, even though Send to Risk Lab and Use my journal can fill one in and run it directly. Use it Use the win rate and reward : risk of your journal (Use my journal) or of a backtest (Send to Risk Lab). |
| Reward to risk | `#lRR` | control | Reward : risk | Reward : risk ● Marginal: needs attention positive expectancy at this win rate Average win ÷ average loss 2 at least 0.1 In plain words How big a win is compared with a loss, in R. At 2 the lab makes each win twice as large as the amount risked. Every loss is exactly the amount risked. Expectancy Expectancy = win rate × reward : risk − (1 − win rate) = 0.45 × 2.00 − 0.55 = +0.35 R per trade. It is the same figure the Expectancy tile shows. Watch out The form checks this field when you press Run: values must be steps of 0.1 from 0.1. A value between steps is refused, even though Send to Risk Lab and Use my journal can fill one in and run it directly. It shows the spread of what luck alone can do to an account that trades the same way. The model Each trade is a win with probability = the win rate: equity × (1 + risk × reward : risk), else equity × (1 − risk). The equity compounds. Costs, slippage and changes of the win rate are not modelled. Watch out Hypothetical paths, not a forecast of your results. Each simulated trade is an independent draw: a win multiplies equity by 1 + risk × reward : risk, a loss by 1 − risk. Break-even at this reward : risk With a reward : risk of 2.00, the win rate that gives zero expectancy is 1 ÷ (1 + 2.00) = 33.3% . Yours is 45%. Watch out Real trades are not independent draws with one fixed win rate, and a win rate measured on a few trades is uncertain. The form checks this field when you press Run: whole numbers, up to 99. ## Opt-outs

From hints-optouts.json. Elements that get no hint card and no hover. Self-explanatory action buttons and what Victor removed (16.11.2026). Owned by T0: a zone task adds candidates to its notes, it does not edit this file. 'selector' is what the engine opts out (the element and everything inside it); the audit marks such elements as opted-out, not as misses. HX.optout(selector) does the same at run time.

|---|---|---|
